questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate shows motile corkscrew-shaped organisms. The causative organism belongs to which order?
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of primary syphilis (chancre), belongs to order Spirochaetales. Dark-field microscopy demonstrates its characteristic corkscrew motility.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on long-term oral contraceptives develops symmetrical hyperpigmentation over the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip that worsens in summer. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of the pigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Melasma (chloasma) presents as symmetrical facial hyperpigmentation, worsened by sun exposure and OCPs. Wood's lamp enhancement indicates epidermal type, which responds better to treatment than the dermal type.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with verrucous plaques on the lower leg for 2 years after a thorn injury. Histopathology shows 'copper-penny bodies' (sclerotic cells). What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis characterized by sclerotic (Medlar/copper-penny) bodies on histology. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice; terbinafine is an alternative. Amphotericin B is used for systemic mycoses.

questions.q: A 30-year-old immunocompromised patient develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along a dermatomal distribution on the left chest wall. Two weeks later, he develops burning pain in the same area despite resolution of rash. What is this complication called?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is persistent pain for >3 months after resolution of herpes zoster rash. It results from nerve damage by VZV reactivation and is more common in elderly and immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) with fever and joint pains. Which cytokine is primarily responsible for ENL reactions?
questions.exp: ENL (Type 2 lepra reaction) is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction in lepromatous leprosy. TNF-alpha is the key mediator. Thalidomide, which inhibits TNF-alpha, is effective treatment.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing skin and mucous membranes. IgG antibodies are directed against desmoglein-3 predominantly. Nikolsky sign is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves IgG against desmoglein-3 (and desmoglein-1). However, this question has a trick - tense bullae with negative Nikolsky is bullous pemphigoid (IgG against BP180/BP230). PV shows flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky. The anti-desmoglein-3 antibody confirms pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral erosions and flaccid bullae. Skin biopsy shows intraepidermal acantholysis with suprabasal split. Direct immunofluorescence shows 'fishnet/chicken wire' pattern of IgG deposition. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid bullae, suprabasal intraepidermal split, positive Nikolsky sign, IgG against desmoglein-3. DIF shows intercellular IgG in fishnet/chicken-wire pattern throughout epidermis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the extensor surfaces of knees and elbows. Histopathology shows elongated rete ridges, suprapapillary thinning, Munro microabscesses, and dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae. What epidermal change is characteristic?
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology characteristically shows parakeratosis (retained nuclei in stratum corneum) combined with hypogranulosis (reduced/absent granular layer). These two features together are pathognomonic of psoriasis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops a malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds. She also has oral ulcers and photosensitivity. ANA is positive (1:1280). Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though it has low sensitivity (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is also specific but can fluctuate with disease activity. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. It has a central ulceration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC (most common type) presents as pearly/translucent papule/nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and may ulcerate centrally ('rodent ulcer'). Most common site is nose. Histology shows palisading of peripheral nuclei.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-colored papules on the penis, perineum, and anal area for 3 months. Examination shows cauliflower-like, soft, moist growths. PCR detects HPV types 6 and 11. What is the first-line patient-applied treatment?
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) caused by HPV 6 and 11. Patient-applied treatments include imiquimod 5% cream (TID, 3×/week) and podophyllotoxin 0.5% (twice daily for 3 days, rest 4 days). Provider-applied: TCA, cryotherapy, surgical removal.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child develops an annular, scaling plaque on the scalp with patchy alopecia. KOH examination shows 'ectothrix' pattern with spores outside the hair shaft. Wood's lamp shows bright green fluorescence. What organism is most likely?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix pattern of tinea capitis (spores around outside of hair shaft) and shows bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Trichophyton tonsurans causes endothrix (no fluorescence). Epidermophyton does not infect hair.

questions.q: A 19-year-old student presents with erythematous, pruritic, edematous wheals that appear and disappear within 24 hours at different sites. Individual lesions do not leave marks. What is the mechanism of this condition?
questions.exp: Acute urticaria is mediated by IgE-dependent activation of mast cells and basophils releasing histamine, causing transient edematous wheals. Each wheal lasts <24 hours and resolves without scarring. Chronic urticaria may have autoimmune mechanisms.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with HIV (CD4: 80 cells/μL) develops painful, ulcerated nodules on the face and extremities. Biopsy shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and HHV-8 on PCR. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: In HIV-associated Kaposi's sarcoma, the primary treatment is HAART (antiretroviral therapy), which often leads to regression. For extensive/symptomatic disease, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (first-line chemotherapy) is used in addition to HAART.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy on multidrug therapy (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) develops methemoglobinemia. Which drug is responsible?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency) and methemoglobinemia. G6PD screening is recommended before dapsone therapy. Rifampicin causes hepatotoxicity and orange discoloration of secretions; clofazimine causes skin discoloration.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with symmetric, indolent plaques with atrophic, porcelain-white center and hyperpigmented borders on the trunk and genitals. Histology shows hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, basal layer liquefaction, and homogenized collagen in papillary dermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus shows characteristic white, atrophic plaques with 'cigarette paper' wrinkling. Histology: epidermal atrophy, basal vacuolation, hyalinized papillary dermis. Genital involvement in women may predispose to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: A surgeon plans excision of a suspected malignant melanoma on the back. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is negative. Histopathology shows Breslow thickness of 1.2 mm. What is the recommended surgical margin?
questions.exp: Excision margins for melanoma: In situ = 0.5–1 cm; Breslow ≤1mm = 1 cm margin; 1.01–2 mm = 1–2 cm margin; >2 mm = 2 cm margin. Breslow 1.2 mm falls in the 1–2 cm category; 1 cm is the minimum recommended.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) with groove sign. He recalls a transient, painless genital ulcer 3 weeks ago. PCR confirms Chlamydia trachomatis. Which serovars are responsible?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. Serovars A-C cause trachoma; D-K cause urogenital chlamydia. The 'groove sign' (groove between inguinal and femoral lymph nodes) is pathognomonic of LGV.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops extensive blistering and skin peeling involving >30% BSA after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. She has conjunctival involvement and mucosal erosions. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN/Lyell's syndrome): >30% BSA epidermal detachment. SJS involves <10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30%. Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, and NSAIDs are common triggers. Nikolsky sign is positive. SCORTEN score guides management.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her first trimester develops pruritic papules and vesicles on the abdomen starting periumbilically. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear C3 along the basement membrane zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigoid gestationis (herpes gestationis): autoimmune subepidermal blistering with IgG and C3 against BP180 (collagen XVII). DIF shows linear C3 at BMZ. Starts periumbilically, spreads. Neonates may also be affected. Treat with topical/systemic steroids.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and calcinosis. She has esophageal dysmotility. ANA is positive with centromere pattern. What antibody is associated with this limited form of scleroderma?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is the limited form of systemic sclerosis. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with CREST/limited SSc. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse SSc and interstitial lung disease.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with recurrent pustular lesions over psoriatic plaques after stopping oral corticosteroids. New lesions appear at sites of skin trauma. What type of psoriasis is this?
questions.exp: Generalized pustular psoriasis (Von Zumbusch) presents with sudden onset of sterile pustules on erythematous skin, fever, and systemic toxicity. Classic trigger is withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response) is positive in psoriasis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with hypopigmented, anesthetic patches over the trunk. Slit-skin smear from lesion is negative. Biopsy shows granulomas around dermal nerves and sweat glands with lymphocytic infiltrate. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT): few, well-defined, hypopigmented, anesthetic patches. AFB negative on smear. Histology shows epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytes around nerve bundles, destroying them. High CMI (Th1 response), Lepromin test strongly positive.

questions.q: During patch testing, a 35-year-old patient shows a reaction at day 2 and day 4 to nickel sulfate, with erythema, papules, and vesicles. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is contact dermatitis?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a classic Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ cells). Reaction occurs 48-96 hours after allergen contact, unlike Type I which is immediate. Patch testing reads at 48h and 96h.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with desquamating erythroderma covering >90% BSA, associated with fever, chills, and hypoalbuminemia. Her past history reveals psoriasis treated with methotrexate which she recently stopped. What is the most dangerous complication?
questions.exp: Erythroderma/exfoliative dermatitis: disrupted thermoregulation causing hypothermia, massive protein loss causing hypoalbuminemia, high-output cardiac failure from increased cutaneous blood flow. Causes include psoriasis, eczema, drug reactions, cutaneous lymphoma.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl has polymorphous eruptions on sun-exposed areas that appear 1-2 hours after sun exposure and resolve within 24 hours. Phototesting shows abnormal response to UVA. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) is the most common photodermatosis, presenting with varied morphology (papules, vesicles, plaques) on sun-exposed skin 1-24 hours after UV exposure. Predominantly UVA-mediated. Treatment: photoprotection, photodesensitization.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with multiple warty, hyperkeratotic lesions on the dorsum of hands and seborrheic keratosis-like lesions on the trunk since childhood. He has palmoplantar keratoderma. This is associated with increased risk of malignancy. What is the inheritance pattern?
questions.exp: Darier's disease (dyskeratosis follicularis) and Cowden syndrome (multiple hamartoma syndrome with PTEN mutation) both show autosomal dominant inheritance. Cowden is associated with breast, thyroid, and endometrial malignancy. The described features suggest epidermodysplasia verruciformis or Cowden syndrome.

questions.q: A drug commonly used for severe psoriasis inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, thereby blocking DNA synthesis. A patient on this drug develops hepatotoxicity after 3 years of therapy. Serial liver biopsies are recommended. What is this drug?
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking DNA synthesis and rapidly dividing cells. Hepatotoxicity (fibrosis, cirrhosis) is cumulative dose-dependent. Liver biopsy is recommended after cumulative dose of 1.5-2g in patients without risk factors. Folic acid supplementation reduces toxicity.

questions.q: A 50-year-old smoker presents with persistent erythematous, scaly plaque on the lower lip for 4 months that does not heal. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without basement membrane breach. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Actinic cheilitis with carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease)
questions.exp: Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) on the lip/actinic cheilitis shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia with intact basement membrane. Risk factors: UV, HPV, arsenic. Treatment: 5-FU, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, or excision. If basement membrane breached, it becomes invasive SCC.

questions.q: A newborn develops a widespread, superficial blistering eruption with Nikolsky sign positive. The baby is febrile and irritable. Culture from the nose of the mother grows Staphylococcus aureus. Histology of blister shows cleavage at the granular layer. What toxin is responsible?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B from S. aureus phage group II. These toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1 at the granular layer, causing superficial blistering. Neonates are more susceptible due to lack of antibodies and immature renal clearance.

questions.q: A patient undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a skin cancer on the nose. This technique involves excision of thin horizontal layers with immediate frozen section examination of 100% of the surgical margins. What is the main advantage of this technique?
opts: It destroys all cancer cells with minimal surgery
It provides the highest cure rate with maximum tissue preservation
It is used only for melanoma
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate for BCC (99% for primary) and SCC while maximizing tissue preservation. By mapping and examining 100% of surgical margins on frozen section, it allows targeted removal of tumor extensions. Indicated for high-risk, recurrent, or anatomically critical site tumors.
